title: Your strategy isn’t what you wrote. It’s what people understood.
author: Zora Artis and Wayne Aspland
summary: Artis argues that the strategic narrative written after a strategy is approved carries more weight than leaders realise, because most employees will never read the strategy deck and will only encounter the story told from it. Writing it is also a test of the strategy, since gaps and contradictions surface when someone first tries to explain the priorities as one story. She recounts uniting a CEO's separate goals with a corporate strategy into one narrative, and contrasts this with a Formula One team where about forty department heads co-created the strategic intent so the narrative described what they already understood. A narrative is only the start, because leaders must tell stories, ask questions, listen and make decisions that point back to it. Her recommendation is to draft the narrative alongside the strategy, test each draft with the executive team, and let the narrative go to the board with the strategy.
points: Most staff meet the strategy only through the narrative, so its quality largely determines understanding and commitment.
If the strategy is hard to explain as one coherent story, fix the strategy before polishing the narrative.
Involving the people who must deliver the strategy in shaping it makes the narrative describe what they already understand.
Leaders bring the narrative to life by explaining hard calls with reference to it, which teaches more than a launch event.
Draft the narrative while the strategy is forming and take both to the board together.
quotes: First up, this narrative represents the first time anyone tries to explain the strategy as one story. That’s usually when gaps start to show.
Second, most employees will never see the 80-page strategy deck the consultants and executive team developed. What they’ll see and hear is the strategic narrative created from it.
Second, creating a strategic narrative is also a test of whether the strategy itself makes sense. Can we explain the priorities clearly? Do they fit together? Are there contradictions?
Because the people responsible for delivering the strategy had shaped it, the narrative described what they already understood and committed to.
A good narrative keeps the substance and makes it meaningful to the people who have to act on it.
When a leader explains a hard call by pointing back to the narrative, people learn more about the strategy than any launch event can teach them.
Where the story is hard to write, the strategy usually needs more work.
